It invites us not to be carried away by our own importance, but to seek humility and dependence on the Lord. As believers, we must always maintain an eternal perspective on our value and our role in the divine plan.

In this verse, it evokes the protection and support that nations found under the shadow of the mighty, indicating a spiritual and physical dependence on this strength.

The word 'Sefer' means book or scroll, often used to refer to the scriptures or documents of the covenant. It symbolizes divine revelation and the authority of God's Word. In the context of this verse, it reminds us of the importance of referring to divine truth to understand our place in the world and our relationship with God.

17.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Israel faced defeat and the loss of their land. It was a time of despair and questioning about God's faithfulness to His people.
17.passage: Ezekiel 31 describes the fall of Assyria, symbolized by a majestic tree that has been cut down. This chapter highlights the fragility of earthly powers in the face of God's sovereignty.
17.culture: In ancient culture, nations were often perceived as trees, symbolizing their strength and influence. The idea of standing in the shadow of a mighty tree evokes the protection and security that can be found in political or military alliances.
17.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that even the powerful, who seemed invincible, ultimately face death and judgment. It reminds us that true security does not lie in human alliances, but in a relationship with God, who alone can offer eternal life.
17.commentaire: This passage urges us to reflect on our own dependencies and what gives us a sense of security. As believers, we must seek our refuge not in the powers of this world, but in the presence of God, who is our true strength and protective shadow. By anchoring ourselves in His Word, we find wisdom and direction to navigate life's trials.

Eden means 'delight' or 'pleasure,' and refers to the Garden of Eden, a symbol of beauty and perfection. In this passage, it evokes an environment of prosperity where Pharaoh compares himself to the trees of Eden, but it also underscores his isolation and downfall, as even the most majestic can be cut down.

18.epoque: This passage takes place in the context of the exile of the people of Israel, where Ezekiel prophesies against the nations, particularly Egypt, which had been a dominant power but would soon face defeat.
18.passage: In Ezekiel 31, the prophet uses the metaphor of a majestic tree to describe the greatness of Pharaoh and his kingdom, while announcing his imminent fall. This chapter highlights the vanity of human glory in the face of God's will.
18.culture: In ancient culture, trees often symbolized strength, longevity, and prosperity. The comparison of Pharaoh to the trees of Eden emphasizes how his glory was perceived as unshakeable, but also how deceptive that perception was.
18.interpretation: This verse reminds us that human glory, even that of the most powerful, is temporary and subject to God's judgment. Pharaoh, despite his greatness, is warned of his fall, illustrating that those who oppose God cannot escape His judgment.
18.commentaire: This passage teaches us humility and recognition of our dependence on God. Human greatness may seem impressive, but it is fragile and fleeting. As believers, we must seek the glory of God rather than that of men, remembering that our worth and security are found in Him alone.
